zh.q: 海面上的水，为什么会自己走成一条条「河」？
zh.concl: 盛行风吹拂海面，推动海水随风漂流，在海洋表层形成规模很大的洋流；洋流方向还受海陆分布和地转偏向力影响。
points: 盛行风吹拂海面，推动海水随风漂流，并使上层海水带动下层海水流动，在海洋表层形成规模很大的洋流。
洋流是「常年比较稳定地沿着一定方向作大规模的流动」，规模远超过河流的流量。
洋流方向还受海陆分布、地转偏向力等因素影响：所以它并不总与风向完全一致。

zh.q: 信风和西风都在推水，为什么中低纬会推成一个圈？
zh.concl: 信风向西推、西风向东推，加上陆地阻挡，中低纬海区才闭合成大洋环流：北半球顺时针、南半球逆时针。
points: 信风把赤道两侧的海水自东向西推到大洋西岸，受陆地阻挡后，大部分海水沿西岸流向较高纬度。
到中纬度海区，在盛行西风吹拂下，洋流转为自西向东流；到大洋东岸又有一部分折向低纬度海区。
这样在中低纬海区闭合成大洋环流：北半球呈顺时针方向流动，南半球呈逆时针方向流动。

zh.q: 同在北半球，中高纬的环流为什么反着转？
zh.concl: 北半球中高纬海区也形成大洋环流，呈逆时针方向流动——因为北侧极地东风向西、南侧盛行西风向东，两支方向相反。
points: 在北半球中高纬度海区也形成大洋环流，它呈逆时针方向流动。
原因在这一带的盛行风：北侧是极地东风（向西南吹），南侧是盛行西风（向东北吹），两支方向相反，环流方向随之反转。
千岛寒流（56°N→37°N，ΔT −8.5 ℃）、拉布拉多寒流、东格陵兰寒流都在这个逆时针环流里；北大西洋暖流是它与中低纬环流共用的那条边（双归属），所以拖到拉布拉多寒流时它仍然亮着。北半球中高纬的 3 条寒流 spinZ 都是 +1，与中低纬的 8 条 −1 反号。

zh.q: 「暖流」「寒流」是按从低纬流向高纬分的吗？
zh.concl: 寒暖按水温判：从水温高的海域流向水温低的海域是暖流，反之是寒流；纬向流本课的温差判据不适用，按教材图例归类。
points: 按海水温度，可以把洋流分为暖流和寒流：从水温高的海域流向水温低的海域的洋流叫暖流，反之叫寒流。
判据是两地的水温之差，不是「从低纬流向高纬」——那只是一种常见情形。
洋流把水体本身搬走，水温随之平流，所以它给经过的海区加热或冷却；这正是暖流增温、寒流降温的原因。

zh.q: 南半球的西风漂流为什么不绕圈？北印度洋的洋流为什么会倒过来流？
zh.concl: 北印度洋的季风洋流随季风反向（冬季向西逆时针、夏季向东顺时针）；南半球的西风漂流终年自西向东、绕南极流动，不是闭合环流。
points: 北印度洋海区冬季盛行东北风，海水向西流动、呈逆时针方向旋转；夏季盛行西南风，海水向东流动、呈顺时针方向旋转。
南半球的西风漂流：南极大陆外围海面广阔，终年受西风影响，自西向东流动，教材没有给它闭合环流。
两条都不成完整的圈，但原因不同：一条是海区被大陆半包围、盛行风随季节反向；一条是海面开阔、终年只受西风影响。

zh.q: 赤道的水最热，为什么盐度却不在赤道最高？
zh.concl: 水温由低纬向高纬递减；盐度以副热带最高、向赤道和两极降低；密度由赤道向两极递增；垂直方向上 1000 m 以内变化大、以下很小。
points: 全球海洋表层水温由低纬向高纬递减；同一海区的表层水温夏季普遍高于冬季（45°N 由 14.5 ℃ 升到 18.2 ℃、45°S 由 18.5 ℃ 降到 14.7 ℃）。
盐度以副热带海域最高，由副热带向赤道和两极逐渐降低：副热带炎热少雨、蒸发大于降水；赤道虽最热，但降水丰沛。
密度由赤道向两极递增：表层海水密度与温度的关系最为密切，温度越高密度越低。

zh.q: 同纬度的东岸和西岸，气候为什么差这么多？
zh.concl: 暖流增温增湿、寒流降温减湿，同纬度大洋东西岸的气温与降水差异由此而来（教材案例：东岸最冷月比西岸高 16—20 ℃）。
points: 暖流使所经海面及附近地区气温偏高、空气暖湿、对流加强，易形成降水；寒流相反：空气稳定，难以致雨。
由于大洋东部和西部洋流性质不同，同纬度大洋东岸和西岸的气温存在差异。
澳大利亚、非洲和南美洲西岸的热带沙漠气候，都与沿岸寒流有关；教材只给「偏高 / 偏低」的定性说法，ΔT_air 的 1.1 倍是课件推算。

zh.q: 世界大渔场为什么正好长在洋流交汇和上升流的地方？
zh.concl: 寒暖流交汇与离岸风上升流都把营养盐带到表层，浮游生物繁盛、鱼类聚集——纽芬兰靠交汇，秘鲁靠上升流。
points: 寒流和暖流交汇处海水扰动强烈，沉积于海底的营养物质上涌，浮游生物繁盛，鱼类聚集，形成大渔场。
秘鲁沿海在东南信风吹拂下表层海水偏离海岸，深部冷水带着海底的营养物质上涌，也形成世界著名渔场。
大渔场的关键是营养盐上涌，不是「水温合适」；纽芬兰渔场 20 世纪 50 年代过度捕捞后鱼群急剧下降，1992 年加拿大禁止捕捞鳕鱼。

zh.q: 考核：教材点名的四个海区，各靠哪一条洋流？
zh.concl: 洋流既决定了大渔场与沿岸气候，也把浅海与远洋连成一片——玩具鸭漂到世界各地，正是这条全球传送带在起作用。
points: 判断一个海区所靠洋流，先看它在哪个大洋、大洋的东岸还是西岸，再看这一侧属于哪一支边界流。
渔场题先问「营养盐从哪来」：交汇还是上升流。
气候题先问「暖流还是寒流」；季风洋流题先问「现在是什么季节」。

en.q: Why does water on the sea surface move on its own in "rivers"?
en.concl: Prevailing winds blow across the sea and make the water drift, forming large surface currents; current direction is also affected by land-sea distribution and the Coriolis force.
points: Prevailing winds blow across the sea, making the water drift with the wind and dragging the lower layers along, forming large currents in the surface ocean.
A current is "a large-scale flow that moves in a fairly stable direction year-round", far larger than any river's discharge.
Current direction is also affected by the distribution of land and sea and the Coriolis force, so it does not always match the wind exactly.

en.q: Trade winds and westerlies both push water. Why do they push it into a loop in low and middle latitudes?
en.concl: Trade winds push west and westerlies push east; with land barriers, the low-middle latitudes close into gyres: clockwise in the north, counterclockwise in the south.
points: The trade winds push water on both sides of the equator westward to the western side of the ocean; blocked by land, most of it flows along the western side toward higher latitudes.
In the middle latitudes the prevailing westerlies turn the current eastward; at the eastern side part of it turns back toward low latitudes.
This closes an ocean gyre in the low-middle latitudes: clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere, counterclockwise in the Southern Hemisphere.

en.tag: Middle-high latitudes turn the other way
en.q: Both in the Northern Hemisphere, why does the middle-high latitude gyre turn the other way?
en.concl: Gyres also form in the northern middle-high latitudes, flowing counterclockwise, because the polar easterlies on the north side blow west and the prevailing westerlies on the south side blow east, in opposite directions.
points: In the middle-high latitudes of the Northern Hemisphere ocean gyres also form, flowing counterclockwise.

The reason is the prevailing winds there: polar easterlies on the north side (blowing southwest) and prevailing westerlies on the south side (blowing northeast) run in opposite directions, so the gyre's direction reverses.

The Oyashio (56°N→37°N, ΔT −8.5 ℃), the Labrador Current and the East Greenland Current are all in this counterclockwise gyre; the North Atlantic Current is the edge it shares with the low-middle latitude gyre (belongs to both), so it stays lit when you drag to the Labrador Current. The 3 cold currents of northern middle-high latitudes all have spinZ +1, opposite to the 8 low-middle latitude currents at −1.

en.q: Are "warm" and "cold" currents defined by flowing from low to high latitude?
en.concl: Warm or cold is judged by water temperature: from warmer to cooler water is a warm current, and the reverse a cold current; this lesson's temperature-difference criterion does not apply to zonal currents, which follow the textbook legend.
points: By water temperature, currents are warm or cold: a current flowing from warmer water to cooler water is a warm current, and the reverse is a cold current.
The criterion is the difference in water temperature between the two places, not "flowing from low to high latitude", which is only a common case.
A current carries the water itself, and its temperature with it, so it warms or cools the areas it passes; that is why warm currents raise temperature and cold currents lower it.

en.q: Why doesn't the West Wind Drift in the Southern Hemisphere form a loop? Why does the current in the northern Indian Ocean reverse?
en.concl: Monsoon currents of the northern Indian Ocean reverse with the monsoon (westward counterclockwise in winter, eastward clockwise in summer); the Southern Hemisphere West Wind Drift flows west to east around Antarctica all year and is not a closed gyre.
points: In the northern Indian Ocean the northeast wind prevails in winter, so the water flows west and rotates counterclockwise; in summer the southwest wind prevails, so the water flows east and rotates clockwise.
The Southern Hemisphere West Wind Drift: the sea around Antarctica is vast and under westerlies all year, so the current flows west to east, and the textbook gives it no closed gyre.
Neither forms a complete loop, but for different reasons: one sea is half-enclosed by land with winds that reverse with the seasons; the other is open sea under westerlies all year.

en.q: Equatorial water is the hottest. Why isn't salinity highest at the equator?
en.concl: Water temperature decreases from low to high latitudes; salinity is highest in the subtropics and lower toward the equator and poles; density increases from equator to poles; vertically, change is large within 1000 m and very small below.
points: Surface ocean temperature decreases from low to high latitudes; in the same area surface water is generally warmer in summer than in winter (45°N rises from 14.5 ℃ to 18.2 ℃, 45°S falls from 18.5 ℃ to 14.7 ℃).

Salinity is highest in the subtropics and decreases toward the equator and the poles: the subtropics are hot and dry with evaporation exceeding precipitation; the equator is hottest but has heavy rainfall.
Density increases from the equator to the poles: surface density is most closely tied to temperature, and warmer water is less dense.

en.q: Why do east and west coasts at the same latitude have such different climates?
en.concl: Warm currents add heat and moisture and cold currents cool and dry, which explains the differences in temperature and rainfall between east and west coasts at the same latitude (textbook case: the coldest month on the east side is 16–20 ℃ warmer than on the west).
points: Warm currents make the sea surface and nearby land warmer, with warm moist air and stronger convection that favors rain; cold currents do the opposite: stable air and little rain.
Because currents on the eastern and western sides of an ocean differ, coasts at the same latitude on either side have different temperatures.

The tropical desert climates on the western coasts of Australia, Africa and South America are all linked to coastal cold currents; the textbook only says "warmer / colder", and the factor of 1.1 for ΔT_air is the lesson's estimate.

en.q: Why are the world's great fishing grounds exactly where currents meet and where upwelling occurs?
en.concl: Warm-cold convergence and offshore-wind upwelling both bring nutrients to the surface, so plankton thrives and fish gather: Newfoundland relies on convergence, Peru on upwelling.
points: Where cold and warm currents meet, the water is strongly stirred, nutrients from the seabed rise, plankton thrives, fish gather, and a great fishing ground forms.
Off Peru the southeast trade winds push surface water away from the coast, and cold deep water rises with seabed nutrients, forming another world-famous fishery.
The key to a great fishery is rising nutrients, not "the right water temperature"; after overfishing in the 1950s the Newfoundland stocks collapsed, and Canada banned cod fishing in 1992.

en.q: Check: which current does each of the four sea areas named in the textbook rely on?
en.concl: Currents shape great fisheries and coastal climates, and also link shallow seas with the open ocean; the toy ducks drifting around the world are this global conveyor belt at work.
points: To find the current a sea area relies on, first see which ocean it is in and whether it is on the eastern or western side, then which boundary current that side has.
For fishery questions, first ask "where do the nutrients come from": convergence or upwelling.
For climate questions, first ask "warm or cold current"; for monsoon current questions, first ask "what season is it".
